item.title: How IT Education Should Be Restructured in the Era of AI Agents
item.description:
I'm teaching a course on AI usage to final-year IT students. I've observed an interesting phenomenon: with an AI agent on a small local Qwen 4B model, I achieve better results than students using agents on top-tier models. The reason isn't so much about AI usage skills as it is about engineering competence. An expert understands the task, narrows down the solution space, manages complexity, detects errors, and provides quality feedback. A novice delegates all this to the model, including decision-making, the correctness of which they cannot assess themselves. Personal expertise is one of the most powerful leverage points for amplifying AI. This raises the question: how should we train developers if a significant portion of coding can now be delegated to agents? Read more

item.title: Anthropic Allows Claude Artifacts to be Installed as Applications on Mac and Windows
item.description:
Developers of desktop software have struggled with packaging, signing, and notarization for years, while Anthropic has hidden all of this behind a single button. On November 24th, Claude for Mac and Windows released the beta 'Install as app'. Now, artifacts can be installed as standalone applications with their own icons and windows. It sounds like a dream, but it's best to read the documentation on permissions first. Read more

item.title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 Model Released: 27 Billion Parameters Compressed to 5.9 GB VRAM
item.description:
Large language models for code have always been bottlenecked by video memory. They require tens of gigabytes of VRAM to run, preferably without compression. The startup PrismML has attempted to solve this problem with ternary quantization in their new Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B model. In its most compact form, Bonsai occupies 5.93 GB of VRAM. According to the company, it solves 75.6% of SWE-bench Verified tasks, compared to 80.6% for Qwen3.8 27B, upon which it was based. Read on for details.

item.title: [Translation] Where is your AI Agent Executing?
item.description:
Ilya Kuchmin, author of the "AI Agents Software Development" course, raises a thought that is difficult to ponder in everyday life: Where is the code that your agent writes actually executed? Over the past year, agent sandboxes have evolved from simple environments for running suspicious code into full-fledged infrastructure. They have snapshots, pause and resume, branching, and even their own browser. But a reverse trend has also emerged: many agents don't need a whole computer at all. If you haven't thought about this yet, now is the time to see where the industry is heading. Read more

item.title: Animating Images: Testing Avatars from Kandinsky, Wan, InfiniteTalk, and FantasyTalking
item.description:
One image, one Russian phrase, and five seconds of video. The task is to animate an image so that the character speaks a phrase I pre-recorded. To do this, the model needs to reproduce articulation, synchronize it with audio, and at the same time preserve the character's recognizability. I decided to test open-source talking avatar generators, but on characters from Russian cultural code. And to make it even more fun – on epic or fairy-tale characters. Because a sculpture's face is carved in stone, bogatyrs have lush beards, and the Grey Wolf is just a wolf. There were no dull moments! One H200, 4 models, and 10 characters – let's go! Read more

item.title: AI Will Destroy Weak Businesses — Who Will Be Affected? And What Happens Next?
item.description:
A plenary discussion "New Economy of Trust: AI, Platforms, and Human-Centricity in the Financial Market" was recently held as part of the Bank of Russia's Fourth Conference "Focus on the Client." I will share my thoughts on the current state of affairs in the world of AI. An interesting story is unfolding with neural networks. There are forecasters who say https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-the that by September of next year, AI will cover the needs of all "white-collar" workers. But the catch is that for effective AI implementation, very structured business processes are needed within an organization. However, not everyone has them. Moreover, it turns out that currently, businesses that are weak and unviable are those where everything is maximally routinized and standardized. If this is your situation, you can prepare for such a business to simply die. Why? Because the transition in business to working with AI and AI agents is not the same as the transition from a typewriter to a computer in its time. The point is different: AI will keep afloat those businesses that are needed by neural networks, not humans. That is, the AI economy, in which humans are simply not needed, is already beginning to emerge. In this economy, everything that is fast and more is valued. More data, more information generated, which no human can sort through due to physical limitations. The internet, social networks, and messengers will enter this AI economy — AI agents, who do not need humans, will communicate there. If a person needs an AI agent to make a decision, then that person's economic agency will disappear. Read more

item.title: How the Creator of Minecraft Became a VibeCoder (and Why You Shouldn't Laugh at Him)
item.description:
If you take two posts by Markus "Notch" Persson on social network X with a four-month gap, you get a perfect meme about the schizophrenia of the modern IT industry. July 14, 2026. The creator of Minecraft posts a concise "Reject AI." The post is met with ovations: over 5 million views and 70,000 likes from grateful engineers tired of the neural network hype. November 23, 2026. The same person on the same platform publicly begs Anthropic to give him more tokens and speed up Claude. He writes that money is not a problem, he is willing to pay any amount because he is creating something unprecedented. Another 4.8 million views. From the outside, it looks like a textbook case of a U-turn. But don't rush to throw rotten tomatoes at Markus. However, if you restore the chronology of his posts from January to November, a much deeper drama unfolds. Persson conducted a four-month experiment on himself live – with all the stages of denial, model hallucinations, good old engineering snobbery, and existential horror about the future of our profession. And the funniest thing is: it seems he hasn't changed his core principles. Read more

item.title: How to Use Brand Rankings in ChatGPT for Promotion in the Runet and What to Check in Your Queries
item.description:
Promoting a website in the Runet cannot be based solely on a brand's position in ChatGPT rankings: it doesn't explain the reason for mentions. The Ahrefs ranking provides hypotheses that need to be tested against your audience's queries. For example, a store name next to a price and instructions for setting up an already purchased product give the brand the same score, although they solve different tasks. Read more

item.title: Project Launched for Collective Deciphering of the Voynich Manuscript Using AI Agents
item.description:
GitHub user Ayan Bandyopadhyay has launched the Voynich Swarm project and a dedicated website for it. The project is an experiment in organizing collective scientific research using a swarm of AI agents attempting to decipher the Voynich manuscript. Anyone can join with their own AI agent. Unlike typical deciphering attempts, the AI agents in Voynich Swarm propose hypotheses, conduct experiments, and verify or refute each other's results. A public research log is maintained, and points are awarded for refuting hypotheses. The infamous Voynich manuscript, created in the early 15th century, contains approximately 38,500 words (if they are words) in an unknown language (if it is a language), illustrations of plants, and astronomical diagrams. It resembles an encrypted diary of a medieval alchemist, herbalist, or botanist, but no universally accepted decipherment exists. The project prompts AI agents with detailed instructions to independently take tasks from a queue, write Python programs, conduct statistical research, and submit results via GitHub. They can also formulate new tasks for other agents. A dedicated 'Red Team' of agents focuses solely on finding errors and refuting conclusions. item.title: How to compare pages from Search Console and AI response monitoring, and why discrepancies don't always mean an error
item.description:
The list of pages from Search Console doesn't have to match AI monitoring: the conditions for a URL to appear in these sources differ. A discrepancy itself doesn't prove a monitoring error. Without actual exports, you can prepare a comparison: save the accounting conditions, match the addresses, and check the disputed pages. Read more
